etymology: Past participle of bind, Old English bindan, to tie fast. A separate line gives the noun bound, a limit or boundary, from Old French bonde. The KJV carries both: the man who is tied, and the line he may not cross.
biblical_def: To be bound in Scripture is to be tied fast—by cord, by oath, by law, by office, or by sin—and the Bible never treats that as a misfortune to be escaped in general terms. It asks instead what a man is bound to, and by whom. Joseph is bound in Egypt; Samson is bound with new cords; Paul is bound in the Spirit unto Jerusalem. The psalmist describes captives bound in affliction and iron (Ps 107:10)—bondage as judgment, from which God alone looses. Marriage is a binding: the woman which hath an husband is bound by the law to her husband so long as he liveth (Rom 7:2), and the binding is what makes the covenant a covenant rather than an arrangement. Christ gives the keys with binding authority attached: whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven (Matt 16:19)—the church's declarations are not private opinions but heaven-ratified acts. Men also bind themselves wickedly: forty Jews bound themselves under a curse to kill Paul (Acts 23:12), an oath so binding they were willing to starve for it. The second sense, bound as boundary, runs alongside: God hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation (Acts 17:26). The whole biblical logic is that a man is always bound to something. The gospel does not deliver him into unboundedness; it transfers the bond—out of the cords of his sins and into the bond of Christ, whose service is freedom.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives BOUND both senses the KJV uses: made fast, tied, obliged or destined; and the limit or external line of a tract or territory.
webster_full: BOUND, pp. — Made fast by a band, or by chains or fetters; obliged by moral ties; confined; restrained.
BOUND, n. — A limit; the external or limiting line of any object or of space; hence a border, a boundary. Thou hast set a bound that they may not pass over (Ps 104:9).
BOUND, a. — Destined; tending; going, or intending to go; as, a man bound for a far country.
scriptures: Matthew 16:19
And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.
Romans 7:2
For the woman which hath an husband is bound by the law to her husband so long as he liveth; but if the husband be dead, she is loosed from the law of her husband.
Psalm 107:10
Such as sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron;
Acts 23:12
And when it was day, certain of the Jews banded together, and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul.
corruption_summary: The age has made bound a synonym for damage. Bonds, limits, obligations and vows are treated as injuries done to the authentic self, and liberation is defined as the absence of anything binding—which Scripture calls not freedom but a different bondage.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic vocabulary has taught a generation to hear bound as trauma. To be bound by a vow, an office, a family, or a moral law is described as being trapped, stifled, or held back; the recommended cure is always the loosening of the tie. In this scheme a man discovers who he is by removing what binds him, and any obligation that survives scrutiny survives only because he chose it this morning and may unchoose it tonight. Scripture makes the opposite claim: identity is constituted by covenant bonds, not discovered underneath them. The husband is not a self who happens to be married; he is bound, and the binding is the man.

The second corruption follows the first: no boundaries is offered as a compliment. But Scripture's God is a God who sets bounds—to the sea, to the nations, to the days of a man—and the removal of bounds is consistently pictured as chaos rather than liberty. Modern usage keeps the word boundaries only in the self-protective sense (limits I impose on others) while discarding it in the submissive sense (limits God imposes on me). The Bible knows only one freedom for a bound creature: to be loosed from sin by being bound to Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew asar, to bind or imprison; Greek deō, to bind or tie fast—the verb behind the keys of the kingdom, the marriage bond, and Paul's chains.
roots_lines: Hebrew asar (H631) — to tie, bind, imprison, or bind oneself by an obligation such as a vow (Gen 42:24; Num 30:2; Judg 16:21).
Greek deō (G1210) — to bind, tie, fasten; used of prisoners' chains, of the marriage bond, and of the binding authority given to the church (Matt 16:19; Rom 7:2; Acts 21:11).
Greek desmios (G1198) — a prisoner, one in bonds; Paul's chosen self-description, the prisoner of Jesus Christ (Eph 3:1; Phm 1:9).
usage: Whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven—church discipline is a binding act, not an opinion poll.
A man is never unbound; he is only bound to something. The question Scripture asks is to whom.
Webster keeps the boundary sense the modern ear has lost: a bound is the limiting line, and God is the one who sets it.

etymology: Old French areer, to put in order, from Latin ad- (to) + a Germanic root meaning to prepare, set in rank. The military sense is the original: an army set in order of battle. The clothing sense is derivative—to be arrayed is to be ordered, not merely covered.
biblical_def: Array in the KJV is a word of rank and order before it is ever a word about clothes. Israel put themselves in array to fight against Benjamin at Gibeah (Judg 20:20); armies are set in array, ranks dressed, each man in his appointed place under a commander. When the word turns to dress it keeps that freight. To be arrayed is to be invested with a station: Joseph arrayed in vestures of fine linen by Pharaoh, Mordecai arrayed in royal apparel, the high priest arrayed in garments made for glory and for beauty. God challenges Job to array thyself with glory and beauty (Job 40:10)—a dare, since only God can clothe a creature in that rank. The Bride's array is granted, not earned or purchased: to her was granted that she should be arrayed in fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints (Rev 19:8). Even the lilies are arrayed, and Solomon in all his glory is not arrayed like one of them—the Lord's argument being that God is the arrayer of His creatures and knows how to clothe them. Wickedness has its array too: the woman of Revelation 17 is arrayed in purple and scarlet, order and splendor bent to rebellion. The word therefore carries the biblical conviction that both armies and garments are matters of assigned order under authority.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ARRAY first as order of battle—the disposition of a body of men in rank—and second as dress or apparel, especially rich or splendid raiment.
webster_full: ARRAY, n. — Order; disposition in regular lines; as an army in battle array. Hence a body of men in order of battle.

ARRAY, v.t. — To place or dispose in order, as troops for battle. Also, to deck or dress; to adorn with dress; it is applied especially to dress of a splendid kind. Array thyself with glory and beauty (Job 40:10).
scriptures: Judges 20:20
And the men of Israel went out to battle against Benjamin; and the men of Israel put themselves in array to fight against them at Gibeah.
Deck thyself now with majesty and excellency; and array thyself with glory and beauty.
Revelation 19:8
And to her was granted that she should be arrayed in fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints.
corruption_summary: Modern usage has kept only the fashion sense of array and dropped the rank behind it, so that clothing becomes self-expression rather than station—dress as a statement about the self rather than a sign of who a man serves and where he stands.
corruption_paragraphs: The Bible's array is assigned. A soldier does not select his position in the line, and a priest does not design his own vestments; both are placed. The modern ear hears array and thinks of a wardrobe, a look, a personal brand—the garment as pure expression of an interior self that owes nothing to any commander. The loss is not aesthetic but structural: when dress no longer signifies station, it can only signify mood, and a culture that dresses by mood has no vocabulary left for the priest's garments, the bride's linen, or the shame of nakedness.

The second loss is the battle sense. Battle array survives as a period phrase in fiction and nowhere in ordinary speech, and with it goes the assumption that ordered ranks under authority are how anything serious gets done. Scripture assumes the opposite of the age: glory is granted from above and worn in rank, and the Bride's fine linen is granted—the one array no one assembles for herself.
roots_summary: Hebrew arak, to set in order or draw up in battle line; Greek periballō, to throw around, to clothe—the verb of the Bride's granted linen.
roots_lines: Hebrew arak (H6186) — to arrange, set in order, draw up in battle array; used of ranks of soldiers and of wood laid in order on the altar (Gen 14:8; Lev 1:7; Judg 20:20).
Greek periballō (G4016) — to throw around, to clothe or array; the verb of the white raiment given to the saints (Rev 3:5; 19:8).
Greek himatizō (G2439) — to clothe with a garment; used of the healed demoniac found sitting, clothed, and in his right mind (Mark 5:15).
usage: The men of Israel put themselves in array—the older and primary sense: ranks dressed for battle.
The Bride's array is granted, not assembled; the fine linen is the righteousness of saints.
Job 40:10 is a dare: array thyself with glory, if thou canst. Only God clothes a creature in that rank.

etymology: Latin proverbium: pro- (forth, before) + verbum (word)—a word put forth, a saying set out in public. Renders Hebrew mashal, a comparison or ruling-word, and Greek paroimia, a byword or figure.
biblical_def: A proverb in Scripture is a compressed ruling-word—Hebrew mashal, from a root that also means to rule. It is wisdom packed tight enough to be carried into a decision, and it governs the man who receives it. Solomon spake three thousand proverbs (1 Kgs 4:32), and the book that bears the name opens by stating its purpose: to understand a proverb, and the interpretation; the words of the wise, and their dark sayings (Prov 1:6). The proverb is deliberately dense; it withholds itself from the careless and yields to the man who will work. The KJV also carries the darker sense, which modern usage has entirely lost: to become a proverb is to become a warning-story other nations tell. Thou shalt become an astonishment, a proverb, and a byword, among all nations (Deut 28:37)—covenant curse expressed as reputation. Christ knows both senses: Ye will surely say unto me this proverb, Physician, heal thyself (Luke 4:23), a saying used as a taunt. So the biblical proverb is never merely a pleasant maxim. It is a short rule that either governs you or is told about you. Proverbs are given to a son by a father, in a covenant household, on the assumption that wisdom is inherited, taught, and obeyed rather than personally discovered.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PROVERB as a short sentence often repeated, expressing a well-known truth; also a byword—a person or thing become the subject of a common saying, usually in reproach.
webster_full: PROVERB, n. — A short sentence often repeated, expressing a well known truth or common fact, ascertained by experience or observation; a maxim of wisdom.
PROVERB, n. — A byword; a name or thing that has become proverbial, generally in reproach. Thou shalt become a proverb and a byword among all nations (Deut 28:37).
scriptures: Proverbs 1:6
To understand a proverb, and the interpretation; the words of the wise, and their dark sayings.
1 Kings 4:32
And he spake three thousand proverbs: and his songs were a thousand and five.
Deuteronomy 28:37
And thou shalt become an astonishment, a proverb, and a byword, among all nations whither the LORD shall lead thee.
Luke 4:23
And he said unto them, Ye will surely say unto me this proverb, Physician, heal thyself: whatsoever we have heard done in Capernaum, do also here in thy country.
corruption_summary: The proverb has been demoted to decoration—a mug slogan, a caption, an inspirational line detached from any authority that could bind the reader—and the covenant-curse sense of becoming a proverb has vanished from the language entirely.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern proverbs are self-issued. Live your truth, follow your heart, no regrets—each has the compressed form of a proverb and none has its function, because a proverb is a ruling-word handed down and these are affirmations handed sideways. Biblical proverbs come from a father to a son with the expectation of obedience; the market's proverbs come from no one in particular and expect nothing. That is why they can be contradictory without embarrassment: nothing rules, so nothing can conflict.

The second loss is the shame sense. Scripture threatens that a disobedient covenant people will become a proverb—a cautionary tale other nations repeat. That usage is gone, and with it the sober awareness that a household, a church, or a nation can end up as the story used to warn others. Keeping only the pleasant half of the word leaves the reader unable to hear Deuteronomy 28 at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew mashal, a comparison or parable, from a root meaning to rule; Greek paroimia, a figure or byword—wisdom compressed until it governs.
roots_lines: Hebrew mashal (H4912) — a proverb, parable, or similitude; cognate with a verb meaning to rule, so that a proverb is a saying that governs (Prov 1:1; 1 Sam 24:13; Ezek 18:2).
Greek paroimia (G3942) — a byword, dark saying, or figure of speech; John's word for Christ's veiled sayings (John 10:6; 16:25, 29; 2 Pet 2:22).
Greek parabolē (G3850) — a parable, comparison, or proverb; the Septuagint's usual rendering of mashal (Luke 4:23).
usage: To understand a proverb, and the interpretation—Proverbs assumes labor, not a glance.
Mashal shares a root with to rule: a proverb is wisdom compressed until it governs.
Deuteronomy 28:37 keeps the lost half of the word: a disobedient people becomes a proverb.

etymology: From charge in the older sense of to load—a charger is a vessel that is loaded, a large dish or platter. Old French chargier, to load, from Late Latin carricare. The war-horse sense is a later and separate development of the same verb, and does not appear in the KJV.
biblical_def: In the KJV a charger is a large serving dish—a platter—and never a horse or a battery. The word appears first in the tabernacle offerings, where each tribal prince brings one silver charger, the weight thereof was an hundred and thirty shekels, filled with fine flour mingled with oil for a meat offering (Num 7:13). Twelve chargers, one per tribe, all identical: the charger is an instrument of ordered, weighed, covenant worship. Ezra records chargers returned among the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had carried off, holy things counted back into their proper use. The word's other appearance is the most infamous in Scripture. Herodias instructs her daughter, and the girl asks Herod, Give me here John Baptist's head in a charger (Matt 14:8); Mark records the request with the same word, in a charger the head of John the Baptist (Mark 6:25). The horror is exact and deliberate: the vessel made for holy offering is used to serve up a prophet's head at a birthday feast. Scripture sets the two uses side by side without comment—the charger that carries fine flour to God, and the charger that carries a murdered man to a dancing girl—and lets the reader feel what a serving dish can be made to do.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives CHARGER first as a large dish or platter, and secondarily as a horse used for attack—the platter being the sense the KJV uses throughout.
webster_full: CHARGER, n. — A large dish or platter. His offering was one silver charger (Num 7:13).
CHARGER, n. — A horse for attack or battle; a war horse. [This later sense is not the KJV usage.]
scriptures: Numbers 7:13

And his offering was one silver charger, the weight thereof was an hundred and thirty shekels, one silver bowl of seventy shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary; both of them were full of fine flour mingled with oil for a meat offering:
Matthew 14:8
And she, being before instructed of her mother, said, Give me here John Baptist's head in a charger.
Mark 6:25
And she came in straightway with haste unto the king, and asked, saying, I will that thou give me by and by in a charger the head of John the Baptist.
corruption_summary: Charger is corrupted mostly by simple drift: the modern reader hears a phone cable or a war-horse, and so misses that the vessel carrying John the Baptist's head is the same kind of vessel that carried fine flour to the altar.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief modern corruption of charger is not ideological but electrical. A reader raised on device cables meets Matthew 14:8 and either pictures nothing or pictures a horse, and either way the scene loses its point. The KJV word is a platter, and the platter is the connection: the same class of serving vessel that appears twelve times over in Numbers 7 loaded with fine flour for God turns up in a Galilean palace loaded with a prophet's head. Herod's feast is a black parody of the tabernacle offering, and the vocabulary is what carries the parody.

There is a further, milder corruption in the reverse direction: readers who do know the war-horse sense import it and imagine something martial in Numbers 7. Keep the order Webster keeps—platter first, horse as a later and separate development. Where a study Bible modernizes to platter, nothing doctrinal is lost; what is lost is the link between the two scenes, which the single KJV word preserves.
roots_summary: Hebrew qe‘arah, a dish or platter of the sanctuary service; Greek pinax, a board, plank, or flat dish—the platter of Herod's feast.
roots_lines: Hebrew qe‘arah (H7086) — a dish or charger, used of the silver platters of the tribal offerings and of the tabernacle vessels (Exod 25:29; Num 7:13-85).
Greek pinax (G4094) — a board or plank, hence a flat dish or platter; used only of the charger bearing John's head and of the dish at the Pharisee's table (Matt 14:8, 11; Mark 6:25, 28; Luke 11:39).
usage: KJV sense is the platter: one silver charger, weighed by the shekel of the sanctuary.
Give me here John Baptist's head in a charger—a worship vessel turned to a birthday atrocity.
The war-horse meaning is later English and never the KJV's; Webster lists the dish first for that reason.

etymology: KJV spelling of entreat: Old French entraiter, en- (in) + traitier (to treat, handle). To intreat is to treat with someone by petition—to plead, and in the passive, to be prevailed upon.
biblical_def: Intreat is the KJV's spelling of entreat, and it means to plead with a person who is able to grant what is asked. Its weight lies in the fact that it is always addressed to someone—never uttered into the air. Pharaoh, broken by the frogs, calls for Moses and says, Intreat the LORD, that he may take away the frogs from me (Exod 8:8): even the hardened king knows that relief comes by petition to a Person. Isaac intreated the LORD for his wife, because she was barren; and the LORD was intreated of him (Gen 25:21)—the same verb active and passive in one verse, which is the heart of the word. To be intreated is to be prevailed upon, to yield to a plea. That God can be intreated is not a small doctrine; it is the ground of all prayer. Eli's terrible question presumes it: if a man sin against the LORD, who shall intreat for him? (1 Sam 2:25)—a cry that finds its answer only in the Mediator. James places the same idea at the center of Christian wisdom, which is easy to be intreated (Jas 3:17): a wise man is approachable, persuadable by a righteous plea, not immovable on principle. The word therefore governs two relationships at once—the creature pleading with God, and the strong man who can be pleaded with.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ENTREAT (KJV intreat) as to ask earnestly, to beseech, to supplicate; and in the passive, to be prevailed upon, to yield to entreaty.
webster_full: ENTREAT, v.t. — To ask earnestly; to beseech; to petition or pray with urgency; to supplicate; to solicit. Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife (Gen 25:21).
ENTREAT, v.i. — To make an earnest petition or request. To be prevailed upon; to yield to entreaty. The Lord was entreated of him.
scriptures: Exodus 8:8

Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron, and said, Intreat the LORD, that he may take away the frogs from me, and from my people; and I will let the people go, that they may do sacrifice unto the LORD.
1 Samuel 2:25

If one man sin against another, the judge shall judge him: but if a man sin against the LORD, who shall intreat for him? Notwithstanding they hearkened not unto the voice of their father, because the LORD would slay them.
James 5:16
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.
corruption_summary: Prayer has been recast as technique—manifesting, visualizing, sending energy—which removes the one thing intreat requires: a Person on the other end who may be prevailed upon and may say no.
corruption_paragraphs: To intreat is to plead with someone. The spiritual market has replaced that with process language: aligning, manifesting, setting an intention, putting it out into the universe. Every one of those phrases is carefully constructed to avoid an addressee, because an addressee has a will and can refuse. Biblical intreaty is riskier and more personal: Pharaoh must ask Moses to ask God; Isaac must plead for a barren wife; the answer is genuinely God's to give. Prayer as technique guarantees a result and abolishes the relationship; prayer as intreaty risks the result and keeps the Person.

A second corruption sits inside the church rather than outside it. James says heavenly wisdom is easy to be intreated—approachable, open to a righteous plea. Modern strength is often defined the opposite way: the leader who cannot be moved, the man who never revisits a decision, immovability marketed as conviction. Scripture distinguishes the two. God Himself is intreated and is not thereby weakened; a father who cannot be intreated by his own children is not strong but hard.
roots_summary: Hebrew athar, to plead and to be prevailed upon; Greek eupeithēs, easily persuaded—the wisdom that is easy to be intreated.
roots_lines: Hebrew athar (H6279) — to pray, supplicate, intreat; in the passive, to be entreated or prevailed upon (Gen 25:21; Exod 8:8; 2 Sam 21:14; 2 Chr 33:13).
Greek parakaleō (G3870) — to call alongside, beseech, exhort, intreat (2 Cor 12:8; 1 Tim 5:1).
Greek eupeithēs (G2138) — easily persuaded, compliant to a plea; the wisdom from above is easy to be intreated (Jas 3:17).
usage: Intreat the LORD—even Pharaoh knows relief comes by petition to a Person, not by technique.
Genesis 25:21 holds both voices of the verb: Isaac intreated, and the LORD was intreated of him.
Heavenly wisdom is easy to be intreated—approachable strength, not immovability.

etymology: Latin concipere: con- (together) + capere (to take)—to take together, to take in. The same verb covers the womb that takes in seed and the heart that takes in a purpose, which is exactly the double use Scripture makes of it.
biblical_def: Scripture uses conceive of the womb and of the heart, and treats the two as one kind of act. In the womb: a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel (Isa 7:14), fulfilled in Gabriel's word to Mary, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son (Luke 1:31). Conception in the Bible is never a merely biological event; it is the point at which God's purpose takes hold in a body. Sarah conceives by promise, Hannah by answered prayer, Elisabeth in old age, Mary by the Holy Ghost. In the heart the same verb runs its darker course: when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death (Jas 1:15). Job says of the wicked, they conceive mischief, and bring forth vanity (Job 15:35). Sin has a gestation. It is conceived in secret, carried, and delivered, and James traces the whole pregnancy so that a man will recognize the early stage rather than only the birth. David confesses conception itself as the point where his sinfulness begins: in sin did my mother conceive me (Ps 51:5). So the word ties together the doctrine of the image, the doctrine of original sin, and the incarnation itself—each turning on what is taken in and what is brought forth.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CONCEIVE as to receive into the womb and become pregnant; and figuratively, to form in the mind, to imagine, devise, or purpose.
webster_full: CONCEIVE, v.t. — To receive into the womb and breed; to begin the formation of the embryo. She shall conceive and bear a son.
CONCEIVE, v.t. — To form in the mind; to imagine; to devise; to purpose. Hence, to conceive mischief is to devise evil in the heart before it is done.
scriptures: Isaiah 7:14
Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
Luke 1:31
And, behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS.
James 1:15
Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.
They conceive mischief, and bring forth vanity, and their belly prepareth deceit.
corruption_summary: Conception has been reduced to a medical event with no moral or covenantal weight, while the heart-sense has been abandoned entirely—leaving no vocabulary for the truth that sin, like a child, is conceived long before it is delivered.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern speech keeps conceive almost exclusively as a clinical term: a procedure succeeded, a cycle worked, a pregnancy was achieved. What drops out is that Scripture treats conception as the moment a person begins and a purpose of God takes hold in a body. Once conception is only biology, the question of what is conceived becomes a matter of preference and timing, and the language required to say otherwise has already been surrendered.

The heart-sense is nearly extinct, and its loss costs the church real ground in the fight against sin. James is precise: lust conceives, carries, and delivers. A man who only recognizes sin at the delivery—the act, the scandal, the fallout—is fighting far too late. The older usage let a man say plainly that he had conceived a bitterness, an adultery, a revenge, weeks before anything was done, and repent at that stage. Recovering the word recovers the early warning.
roots_summary: Hebrew harah, to conceive or be with child, used of wombs and of wicked schemes alike; Greek syllambanō, to take together, to conceive.
roots_lines: Hebrew harah (H2029) — to conceive, become pregnant; also used of conceiving mischief or trouble in the heart (Gen 4:1; Ps 7:14; Isa 7:14; 59:4).
Greek syllambanō (G4815) — to take together, seize; hence to conceive in the womb (Luke 1:24, 31, 36) and, in James, of lust conceiving (Jas 1:15).
Greek gennao (G1080) — to beget or bring forth, the delivery that follows conception (Matt 1:20; Jas 1:15 context).
usage: A virgin shall conceive—the incarnation itself hangs on this verb.
James 1:15 gives sin a full pregnancy: conceived by lust, carried, delivered as death.
Job's wicked conceive mischief—the heart is a womb, and it is never idle.

etymology: From Old French censier, a shortened form of encensier, from Latin incensum, that which is burned. A censer is the pan that carries burning incense—fire and fragrance together, in a vessel God specified.
biblical_def: A censer is the vessel that carries fire and incense before God, and in Scripture it is never a neutral piece of equipment. Every appearance turns on whether the man holding it was authorized. Nadab and Abihu took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not (Lev 10:1)—and fire from the LORD devoured them. Their sin was not carelessness with a utensil; it was worship God had not commanded, offered by men He had not sent. Korah's rebellion is fought with censers: Take you censers, Korah, and all his company (Num 16:6), a test of who may draw near, and the earth opens on the answer while the censers themselves are hammered into a covering for the altar as a permanent memorial. The high priest's censer is at the center of the Day of Atonement, the cloud of incense covering the mercy seat that he die not. Hebrews lists the golden censer among the holy things of the second tabernacle (Heb 9:4). And heaven still has one: an angel stands at the altar having a golden censer, and the incense is offered with the prayers of all saints (Rev 8:3), after which the same censer is filled with altar fire and cast to the earth in judgment. The censer therefore says two things at once—that God receives the prayers of His people, and that access is on His terms.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CENSER as a vase or pan in which incense is burned—among the Jews, a vessel of the sanctuary service used for carrying fire and incense before the LORD.
webster_full: CENSER, n. — A vase or pan in which incense is burned. Among the Jews, a kind of chafing dish or fire-pan of the sanctuary, used for burning incense before the Lord. Nadab and Abihu took either of them his censer (Lev 10:1).
scriptures: Leviticus 10:1
And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not.
Numbers 16:6
This do; Take you censers, Korah, and all his company;
Revelation 8:3

And another angel came and stood at the altar, having a golden censer; and there was given unto him much incense, that he should offer it with the prayers of all saints upon the golden altar which was before the throne.
Hebrews 9:4
Which had the golden censer, and the ark of the covenant overlaid round about with gold, wherein was the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron's rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant;
corruption_summary: Worship has been redefined as sincerity plus atmosphere, which is precisely the assumption the censer passages destroy: Nadab, Abihu and Korah all brought real fire, real incense and real zeal, and God had not commanded it.
corruption_paragraphs: The contemporary rule is that God accepts whatever is offered with a sincere heart. The censer texts say otherwise with unusual bluntness. Nadab and Abihu brought genuine fire and genuine incense in the proper vessels; the single defect was that the LORD commanded them not. Korah's two hundred and fifty men were not atheists but enthusiasts who wanted access God had assigned elsewhere. Neither story can be read as a warning against insincerity, because insincerity is not what happened. They are warnings against unauthorized worship—a category the modern church has largely stopped believing in.

The second corruption is aesthetic. Where incense and censers survive in modern usage, they usually signify mood: a vibe, an ambience, a sense of the numinous available on demand. Scripture's censer is bound to atonement and to mediation. In Revelation the incense rises with the prayers of all saints, and the same censer that carries prayer up is filled with fire and thrown down in judgment. Ambience has no such double edge.
roots_summary: Hebrew machtah, a fire-pan or censer of the sanctuary; Greek libānōtos, the golden censer of Revelation—fire, incense, and the prayers of the saints.
roots_lines: Hebrew machtah (H4289) — a fire-pan, snuff-dish, or censer used in the tabernacle service (Exod 27:3; Lev 10:1; 16:12; Num 16:6-39).
Hebrew miqtereth (H4730) — a censer for burning incense (2 Chr 26:19; Ezek 8:11).
Greek libānōtos (G3031) — frankincense, and by extension the golden censer that carries it (Rev 8:3, 5).
usage: Strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not—the defect was authorization, not sincerity.
Korah's censers were beaten into altar plating: a permanent memorial that access is God's to assign.
Revelation 8 keeps the censer in heaven, carrying the prayers of all saints.

etymology: Latin polluere, to defile or soil, from por- (forth) + luere (to smear). In the KJV the smearing is moral and ceremonial: what God has made holy is dragged into common or filthy use.
biblical_def: To pollute in Scripture is to defile what God has declared holy—to take a thing set apart and treat it as common or filthy. The objects of the verb are almost always God's own: His sabbaths, His sanctuary, His altar, His name, His land, His covenant. My sabbaths they greatly polluted (Ezek 20:13) is the charge against a rebel generation. The priests of Malachi's day polluted the altar with contemptible offerings and then asked innocently, Wherein have we polluted thee? (Mal 1:7). Zephaniah's indictment is blunt: her priests have polluted the sanctuary, they have done violence to the law (Zeph 3:4). The land itself can be polluted, and by a specific sin: ye shall not pollute the land wherein ye are: for blood it defileth the land: and the land cannot be cleansed of the blood that is shed therein, but by the blood of him that shed it (Num 35:33)—innocent blood stains ground, and only justice removes the stain. Notice what pollution is not in the Bible: it is not primarily dirt, disease, or environmental damage. It is a relational and covenantal category. A thing is polluted when it is used against the purpose for which God sanctified it, and the pollution attaches to worship, to marriage, to the priesthood, to the name of God, and to the ground itself.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines POLLUTE as to make foul or unclean; to defile; and specifically to profane—to apply to a common purpose that which is holy, or to violate by irreverence.
webster_full: POLLUTE, v.t. — To make foul or unclean; to defile; in a general sense.
POLLUTE, v.t. — To taint with guilt; to profane; to use for a common purpose what is holy or set apart. They polluted my sabbaths (Ezek 20:13). Also, to violate by illegal sexual commerce.
scriptures: Ezekiel 20:13

But the house of Israel rebelled against me in the wilderness: they walked not in my statutes, and they despised my judgments, which if a man do, he shall even live in them; and my sabbaths they greatly polluted: then I said, I would pour out my fury upon them in the wilderness, to consume them.
Malachi 1:7
Ye offer polluted bread upon mine altar; and ye say, Wherein have we polluted thee? In that ye say, The table of the LORD is contemptible.
Zephaniah 3:4
Her prophets are light and treacherous persons: her priests have polluted the sanctuary, they have done violence to the law.
corruption_summary: Pollution has been narrowed to an environmental measurement, so that a culture can speak fluently about polluted air and have no words at all for a polluted altar, a polluted marriage bed, or a land defiled by innocent blood.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern word is a matter of parts per million. Pollution is what industry does to water; it is measured, regulated, and morally weightless apart from the statute. Scripture's pollution is a covenant category—something holy dragged into common use—and it cannot be measured by instruments at all. The narrowing is convenient: a society that only recognizes chemical defilement can pride itself on clean rivers while its worship, its marriages, and its courts are precisely what the prophets called polluted.

A second corruption is the confident denial that anything can be defiled, because nothing is holy in the first place. If the sabbath is a preference, it cannot be profaned; if marriage is a contract, it cannot be defiled; if the sanctuary is a building, it cannot be polluted. Malachi's priests were more sophisticated than that. They did not deny the categories; they asked, Wherein have we polluted thee?—the tone of men who kept the vocabulary and had stopped believing the substance, which is nearer to the church's present danger than open denial.
roots_summary: Hebrew chalal, to profane or make common, and tame, to make unclean—the two verbs behind sabbaths profaned, sanctuaries defiled, and land stained by blood.
roots_lines: Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to profane, defile, make common; used of profaning the sabbath, the sanctuary, the priesthood, and the name of God (Lev 19:8; Ezek 20:13; 22:26).
Hebrew tame (H2930) — to be or become unclean, to defile ceremonially or morally (Lev 11:44; Num 35:34; Ezek 20:31).
Hebrew chaneph (H2610) — to be profaned or polluted, especially of land defiled by bloodshed (Num 35:33; Ps 106:38; Isa 24:5).
usage: My sabbaths they greatly polluted—pollution in Scripture attaches first to holy things.
Wherein have we polluted thee? is the voice of men who kept the words and lost the substance.
Numbers 35:33: innocent blood defiles the ground, and only justice cleanses it.

etymology: Old English begietan, to get, obtain, or procreate: intensive be- + gietan (to get). The English keeps the plain force—to father, to bring into being—and the KJV uses it for genealogy, for regeneration, and for the eternal generation of the Son.
biblical_def: To beget is to father. The word carries the genealogies—Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob (Matt 1:2)—and those lists are not filler; they are the covenant tracked through actual men. Genesis 5 states the pattern at the fall's edge: Adam lived an hundred and thirty years, and begat a son in his own likeness, after his image (Gen 5:3), which is a deliberate echo and downgrade of the image language of Genesis 1. Fathers transmit likeness, and after Eden that likeness includes death. The verb then rises to two higher uses. First, the eternal generation of the Son: Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee (Ps 2:7), and John's the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father (John 1:18). The Son is begotten, not made—of the same nature as the Father, not a creature produced out of nothing. The church fought for that distinction, and this verb is where it lives. Second, regeneration: believers are begotten again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead (1 Pet 1:3), and James says of his own will begat he us with the word of truth (Jas 1:18). New birth is God's fathering, not the sinner's decision to be born. So beget holds together three doctrines: that human fatherhood transmits both image and fallenness, that the Son is eternally of the Father's nature, and that salvation is a birth a man does not perform on himself.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BEGET as to procreate, as a father or sire; to generate; and figuratively, to produce as an effect or to cause to exist.
webster_full: BEGET, v.t. — To procreate, as a father or sire; to generate. Abraham begat Isaac.
BEGET, v.t. — To produce as an effect; to cause to exist; to generate; as, luxury begets vice.
scriptures: Genesis 5:3
And Adam lived an hundred and thirty years, and begat a son in his own likeness, after his image; and called his name Seth:
Matthew 1:2
Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren;
Psalm 2:7
I will declare the decree: the LORD hath said unto me, Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee.
John 1:18
No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.
corruption_summary: Fatherhood has been reclassified as an optional role rather than a generative act, and begotten has been flattened into a synonym for created—a translation choice with the Arian controversy sitting directly underneath it.
corruption_paragraphs: The cultural corruption is the demotion of begetting. A father is increasingly described as whoever performs the caregiving function, with the act of fathering treated as biologically trivial and socially interchangeable. Scripture will not have it: the genealogies exist precisely because who begot whom is covenantally decisive, and Genesis 5 says a son bears his father's likeness and image. That is not sentiment about resemblance; it is the mechanism by which both the image of God and the fall travel through history.

The doctrinal corruption is quieter and older. Render only begotten as merely one and only or unique, and the word that distinguishes the Son from every creature goes soft. Begotten means of the same nature as the one who begets; made means brought into being out of nothing. Arius was content with a unique Son so long as that Son was made. The Nicene fathers insisted on begotten, not made because this single verb carries the deity of Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew yalad, to bear or beget; Greek gennaō, to beget or bring forth, and monogenēs, only begotten—the words behind genealogy, generation, and regeneration.
roots_lines: Hebrew yalad (H3205) — to bear, bring forth, beget; the verb driving the genealogies of Genesis and the promise of Psalm 2:7 (Gen 5:3; 10:8; Ps 2:7).
Greek gennaō (G1080) — to beget, of the father; to bring forth, of the mother; used of natural generation, of Christ's begetting, and of the new birth (Matt 1:2; John 3:3; 1 John 5:1).
Greek monogenēs (G3439) — only begotten, sole-born of its kind; used of Isaac and of Christ (John 1:14, 18; 3:16; Heb 11:17).
usage: Begat a son in his own likeness, after his image—fathers transmit likeness, and after Eden that includes death.
Begotten, not made: this verb is where the deity of the Son is defended.
James 1:18 — new birth is God's fathering; no man begets himself.

etymology: From Old French chastier, from Latin castigare: castus (pure) + agere (to make, drive)—literally to make pure. Correction aimed at cleansing, not at venting.
biblical_def: Chastise is corrective discipline administered by an authority who loves the one corrected and intends his good. The etymology—to make pure—is the biblical sense exactly. Hebrews states the doctrine plainly: whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth (Heb 12:6), and then turns the argument in a direction the modern reader rarely expects: if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons (Heb 12:8). The absence of correction is not evidence of favor but of no relationship at all. Fathers are commanded into the same office: he that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes (Prov 13:24)—and betimes matters, meaning early, before the fault hardens. God chastises corporately too: I, even I, will chastise you seven times for your sins (Lev 26:28), the covenant curses functioning as escalating discipline meant to drive a people back rather than merely to punish them. Scripture is careful about the shape of it. Chastisement is measured, purposeful, temporary, administered by one with the right to administer it, and aimed at holiness—that we might be partakers of his holiness (Heb 12:10). It is neither abuse (which is rage using discipline as cover) nor indulgence (which is the withholding Proverbs calls hatred). Even Pilate's cynical I will therefore chastise him, and release him (Luke 23:16) borrows the vocabulary of correction to describe a scourging with no righteous purpose in it at all.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CHASTISE as to correct by punishment; to punish for the purpose of reclaiming an offender; to inflict pain for the purpose of correction or reformation.
webster_full: CHASTISE, v.t. — To correct by punishing; to punish; to inflict pain by stripes, or in other manner, for the purpose of punishing an offender and recalling him to his duty. I will chastise you seven times for your sins (Lev 26:28).
CHASTISE, v.t. — To reduce to order or obedience; to restrain; to awe; to correct. Hence, to purify, as by discipline.
scriptures: Hebrews 12:6
For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.
Hebrews 12:8
But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons.
Proverbs 13:24
He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes.
Leviticus 26:28
Then I will walk contrary unto you also in fury; and I, even I, will chastise you seven times for your sins.
corruption_summary: The age has collapsed chastisement into abuse at one end and permissiveness at the other, treating all corrective pain as trauma—so that Hebrews 12, which calls the absence of chastening a mark of bastardy, has become nearly unreadable.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant corruption identifies all discipline with violence. Any imposed consequence is reframed as harm done to a developing self, and correction is replaced with negotiation, accommodation, or referral. There is a real abuse the church must name and refuse: rage that calls itself correction, punishment that serves the punisher, discipline unmoored from love and proportion. Scripture condemns that as loudly as anyone, forbidding fathers to provoke their children to wrath. But it condemns the opposite too, and with a sharper word: the father who spares the rod hateth his son. Withholding correction is not gentleness; Proverbs classifies it as hatred, because it abandons a child to his own folly.

The second corruption runs the other way and is common in religious homes: chastisement as temper with a verse attached. The biblical form is measured, early (betimes), explained, and aimed at holiness rather than at compliance or at the parent's relief. Hebrews 12:10 supplies the test—earthly fathers chastened after their own pleasure, but God for our profit. Any correction that serves the corrector's pleasure has already left the biblical category, whatever text is quoted over it.
roots_summary: Hebrew yasar, to discipline or instruct by correction; Greek paideuō, to train a child—the verb behind Hebrews 12 and the root of pedagogy.
roots_lines: Hebrew yasar (H3256) — to chasten, discipline, instruct; the noun musar is the instruction Proverbs urges a son to receive (Deut 8:5; Prov 13:24; 19:18; Lev 26:28).
Greek paideuō (G3811) — to train or instruct a child, hence to chastise as part of upbringing; the whole argument of Hebrews 12:5-11 (Eph 6:4; 2 Tim 3:16; Titus 2:12).
Greek mastigoō (G3146) — to scourge; the intensifying verb of Hebrews 12:6, scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.
usage: Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth—correction is evidence of sonship, not of rejection.
If ye be without chastisement... then are ye bastards, and not sons—Hebrews 12:8 inverts the modern instinct.
Proverbs 13:24 calls the withholding of the rod hatred, and requires it betimes—early.

etymology: Greek baptizō, to dip, immerse, or plunge, from baptō, to dip. The English word is a transliteration rather than a translation, which is why the argument over its meaning has never been settled by the English alone.
biblical_def: To baptize is to wash by immersion into—and in the New Testament the crucial question is always into what. The Great Commission gives the formula: teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost (Matt 28:19). Baptism is a commanded act of the church, not an optional ceremony, and it is trinitarian at its core. Peter joins it to repentance and remission at Pentecost: Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins (Acts 2:38). Paul explains its meaning as union with Christ in His death and resurrection: we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life (Rom 6:4). The sign matches the thing signified—down into the water as into the grave, up out of it as into new life. Peter guards it from superstition even while saying it saves: baptism doth also now save us (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God,) by the resurrection of Jesus Christ (1 Pet 3:21). The water does not scrub the soul; the resurrection does, and baptism is the appointed answer of a conscience laying hold of it. Baptism is also public allegiance: a man baptized has visibly changed sides, which is why in hostile settings it, and not private belief, is what draws the persecution.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BAPTIZE as to administer the sacrament of baptism—to wash with water as a religious rite, and by extension to christen or name at baptism.
webster_full: BAPTIZE, v.t. — To administer the sacrament of baptism to; to wash with water as a religious ceremony and rite of initiation into the visible church. Go ye therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them (Matt 28:19).
BAPTISM, n. — The application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ceremony, by which he is initiated into the visible church of Christ.
scriptures: Matthew 28:19
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Romans 6:4
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.
Acts 2:38
Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
1 Peter 3:21
The like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God,) by the resurrection of Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: Baptism is corrupted in two opposite directions: reduced to a sentimental family photo-op with no doctrine attached, or inflated into a mechanical rite that saves apart from faith—while the commanded, public, allegiance-declaring character of it drops out of both.
corruption_paragraphs: The sentimental corruption is the more common in the modern West. Baptism becomes an occasion—a naming ceremony, a family gathering, a milestone photograph—detached from repentance, from union with Christ's death, and from membership in a visible church that will now hold the baptized accountable. Whatever a reader concludes about the proper subjects and mode of baptism, Scripture never presents it as a private family sentiment. It is the church's commanded act of initiating a disciple.

The mechanical corruption runs the other way: the rite treated as automatically regenerating, so that the water does the work whatever the state of the heart. Peter forecloses that reading in the very verse where he says baptism saves—not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God, by the resurrection of Jesus Christ. A third corruption, subtler and newer, is aesthetic: baptism as content, staged and filmed for an audience. The New Testament's public dimension is a declaration of allegiance before witnesses who may make you pay for it—not a performance for an audience that will applaud.
roots_summary: Greek baptizō, to immerse or plunge, from baptō, to dip—transliterated rather than translated into English, hence the long argument over mode.
roots_lines: Greek baptizō (G907) — to dip, immerse, submerge; used of John's baptism, Christian baptism, and figuratively of being overwhelmed (Matt 3:6; Mark 10:38; Acts 2:38; Rom 6:3).
Greek baptō (G911) — to dip, the simple verb behind baptizō (Luke 16:24; John 13:26; Rev 19:13).
Greek baptisma (G908) — baptism, the rite itself; Paul's one Lord, one faith, one baptism (Eph 4:5; Rom 6:4; 1 Pet 3:21).
usage: Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost—commanded, and trinitarian.
Romans 6:4 gives the meaning: buried with Him, raised to walk in newness of life.
1 Peter 3:21 guards the sign: not the washing of flesh, but the answer of a good conscience.

etymology: Latin murmurare, to mutter or rumble—an imitative word, the sound of a low continuous complaint. The form itself is the definition: not a shout, but a grumble passed along under the breath.
biblical_def: Murmuring is low, spreading complaint against God's provision and against the leaders He appointed, and Scripture treats it as one of the gravest and most contagious sins of the covenant people. Its home is the wilderness: the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness (Exod 16:2)—days after the Red Sea, over bread. God hears it as directed at Himself: How long shall I bear with this evil congregation, which murmur against me? I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel (Num 14:27). The murmur is aimed at Moses; God receives the invoice. Paul makes the wilderness a standing warning to the church: Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer (1 Cor 10:10). And the positive command is stark in its scope: Do all things without murmurings and disputings (Phil 2:14)—all things, which leaves no exempt category of grievance. Jude describes the ungodly as murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts (Jude 16). Two distinctions keep this from becoming cruelty. Murmuring is not lament: the Psalms complain loudly and directly to God, and that is faith speaking. Murmuring is not the lawful bringing of a real grievance to those responsible, as in Acts 6 where a genuine murmuring over neglected widows is answered by structural remedy rather than rebuke. Murmuring is complaint that travels sideways—never to God, never to the man who could fix it, always to the man who cannot.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MURMUR as a low sound continued or continually repeated; and as a complaint half suppressed or uttered in a low muttering voice—grumbling, expressed discontent.
webster_full: MURMUR, n. — A low sound continued or continually repeated, as that of a stream running in a stony channel, or that of flame.
MURMUR, v.i. — To grumble; to complain; to utter complaints in a low, half articulated voice; to utter sullen discontent. The people murmured against Moses (Exod 15:24).
scriptures: Exodus 16:2
And the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness:
Numbers 14:27
How long shall I bear with this evil congregation, which murmur against me? I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel, which they murmur against me.
1 Corinthians 10:10
Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer.
Philippians 2:14
Do all things without murmurings and disputings:
corruption_summary: Murmuring has been rebranded as authenticity—venting, processing out loud, speaking one's truth—so that the precise sin Scripture says destroyed a generation now presents itself as honesty and even as courage.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern reclassification is nearly total. Sustained sideways complaint is called venting, processing, speaking up, or being real, and the man who does it is praised for not bottling things up. Scripture's category is narrower and more searching. Murmuring is not defined by volume or by emotion but by direction: it goes sideways rather than upward or forward. Israel's complaint was factually accurate—there was no bread—and God still called it evil, because the accurate grievance was carried to everyone except the One who had just parted a sea.

The church must guard the opposite ditch as well. Some leaders use murmuring as a muzzle, labeling any criticism as rebellion and any question as Korah. Acts 6 refutes that outright: a real murmuring over neglected Hellenist widows is met not with a sermon on grumbling but with seven men appointed to fix the neglect. And the Psalms are full of complaint so raw it embarrasses modern piety—addressed to God, which is what makes it prayer instead of murmuring. The test is not whether a man has a grievance. It is where he takes it.
roots_summary: Hebrew lun, to murmur or grumble, the wilderness word; Greek gogguzō, an onomatopoeic verb for muttering—the sound of complaint moving through a crowd.
roots_lines: Hebrew lun (H3885) — to murmur, grumble, complain; the characteristic verb of the wilderness generation (Exod 15:24; 16:2; Num 14:2, 27).
Greek gogguzō (G1111) — to mutter, murmur, grumble in a low tone; used of the Jews murmuring at Christ's words and of the church's forbidden complaining (John 6:41; 1 Cor 10:10; Phil 2:14).
Greek goggusmos (G1112) — a murmuring, secret displeasure; including the lawful grievance of Acts 6:1 that was answered by remedy (John 7:12; Acts 6:1; 1 Pet 4:9).
usage: I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel—aimed at Moses; received by God.
Do all things without murmurings and disputings—Philippians leaves no exempt grievance.
Lament goes up to God; murmuring goes sideways to the man who cannot fix it.

etymology: Latin persuadere: per- (thoroughly) + suadere (to advise, urge as good). To persuade is to bring a man thoroughly to see a thing as good—by reasoning, not by force.
biblical_def: Persuade in the New Testament is the apostolic method: winning a mind by truth openly stated. Luke's summary of Paul at Corinth is typical—he reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath, and persuaded the Jews and the Greeks (Acts 18:4). Not manipulated, not pressured, not entertained: reasoned with and persuaded. Paul states the motive with unusual nakedness: Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men (2 Cor 5:11)—the persuasion is urgent because judgment is real, and it is aimed at men because men have minds that can be addressed. Agrippa's famous half-yielding, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian (Acts 26:28), shows the process failing at the threshold, and Paul does not respond by escalating pressure. Galatians supplies the boundary: For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ (Gal 1:10)—persuasion that shifts its content to win approval has stopped being persuasion and become flattery. The verb also has a passive sense that runs deep in Paul: I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life... shall be able to separate us from the love of God (Rom 8:38-39). Christian assurance is a settled persuasion, a mind convinced, not a mood sustained. Truth persuades; the Spirit convinces; the preacher reasons.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PERSUADE as to influence by argument, advice, or entreaty—to bring the mind to assent; distinguished from convincing, which addresses the understanding alone.
webster_full: PERSUADE, v.t. — To influence by argument, advice, entreaty or expostulation; to draw or incline the will to a determination by presenting motives to the mind.
PERSUADE, v.t. — To convince by argument or reasons offered; to convince of the truth of a proposition. Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian (Acts 26:28).
scriptures: Acts 18:4
And he reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath, and persuaded the Jews and the Greeks.
2 Corinthians 5:11
Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men; but we are made manifest unto God; and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences.
Acts 26:28
Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian.
Galatians 1:10
For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
corruption_summary: Persuasion has been replaced on one side by manipulation—the engineered nudge, the algorithmic feed, the manufactured consensus—and abandoned on the other by a relativism that says nothing can be argued because everyone has his own truth.
corruption_paragraphs: The manipulative corruption is now an industry. Persuasion in the marketing and political sense means bypassing the reasoning mind: framing, priming, social proof, repetition, outrage. What is technically achieved is compliance, not conviction, and the difference matters, because a man moved without his understanding can be moved back the same way tomorrow. Paul's method is the opposite. He reasons in the synagogue, in the market, before governors, and lets men say no—as Agrippa nearly does—because a persuasion that could not have been refused was never persuasion.

The relativist corruption is the mirror image: since nothing is true for everyone, persuasion is recast as aggression and any attempt to change a mind becomes an imposition on identity. That would render the New Testament unintelligible. Paul persuades because the terror of the Lord is real and men's minds are not sealed compartments. Within the church a third corruption appears—persuasion that adjusts its content to be liked. Galatians 1:10 names it: a man who trims to please men has ceased to be the servant of Christ, however persuasive he has become.
roots_summary: Greek peithō, to persuade, and in the passive, to be persuaded, to trust—the same root that gives pistis, faith.
roots_lines: Greek peithō (G3982) — to persuade, prevail upon; in the perfect passive, to be persuaded, to have confidence, to trust (Acts 18:4; 26:28; Rom 8:38; Gal 1:10; Heb 13:18).
Greek pistis (G4102) — faith; from the same root as peithō, so that faith is a persuaded confidence rather than a leap in the dark (Rom 10:17; Heb 11:1).
Greek dialegomai (G1256) — to reason, discourse, dispute; Paul's companion verb to persuading (Acts 17:2; 18:4; 19:8).
usage: He reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath, and persuaded—the apostolic method is argument, not pressure.
Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men—urgency without manipulation.
Galatians 1:10 draws the line: persuasion that trims to please men is flattery.

etymology: English part + taker—one who takes a part, a sharer. It renders Greek koinōnos and metochos, words of fellowship and shared possession, and the KJV uses it for holy sharing and for guilty sharing alike.
biblical_def: A partaker is one who takes a share, and Scripture uses the word with unnerving evenhandedness: a man may be a partaker of Christ or a partaker of evil deeds, and the mechanism is the same. On the high side: we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end (Heb 3:14), and Peter's astonishing promise that by God's precious promises ye might be partakers of the divine nature (2 Pet 1:4)—not deification, but real participation in the holiness and life of God. Communion is partaking in the most literal sense: the cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? (1 Cor 10:16), and Paul continues by insisting a man cannot partake at the Lord's table and at the table of devils. Then the warning side, which is where the Godspeed text lives: he that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds (2 John 11). To greet a false teacher with the blessing of a fellow-worker is to take a share in his work. Paul says the same about hasty ordination—neither be partaker of other men's sins (1 Tim 5:22)—and Revelation calls God's people out of Babylon that ye be not partakers of her sins. The doctrine underneath is that fellowship transmits. A man becomes what he shares in.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PARTAKER as one who has or takes a part, share, or portion in common with others; a sharer; also an accomplice, an associate in guilt.
webster_full: PARTAKER, n. — One who has or takes a part, share or portion in common with others; a sharer; as a partaker of the divine nature.
PARTAKER, n. — An accomplice; an associate. Be not partaker of other men's sins (1 Tim 5:22).
scriptures: 2 Peter 1:4
Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust.
1 Corinthians 10:16
The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
2 John 1:11
For he that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds.
Hebrews 3:14
For we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end;
corruption_summary: Fellowship has been reduced to sociability—community as a warm feeling with no doctrinal content and no transfer of guilt—which empties both the Lord's table and John's warning that greeting a false teacher makes a man a partaker of his deeds.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern community means proximity plus warmth. It asks what a group feels like, not what it shares in. Biblical partaking is a transfer: at the Lord's table a believer genuinely shares in the body and blood of Christ, and Paul argues from that reality that the same man cannot also share at the table of devils. Where fellowship is only sociability, the whole argument collapses, and the Supper becomes a memorial gesture among friends rather than the participation Paul says it is.

The second corruption is the denial that association transmits anything. Endorsement is treated as costless, platform-sharing as neutral, and the man who declines to bid a false teacher God speed is called unloving. Second John says flatly that the greeting makes the greeter a partaker of the evil deeds. This is not a warrant for suspicion of every neighbor or for refusing ordinary civility; John's target is the man who denies that Christ came in the flesh and comes seeking the church's welcome. But it does mean the modern instinct—that a warm public greeting commits a man to nothing—is exactly what the apostle denies.
roots_summary: Greek koinōnos, a sharer or partner, and metochos, one who holds with another—the vocabulary of communion, and of complicity.
roots_lines: Greek koinōnos (G2844) — a partner, sharer, associate; used of partners in the gospel and of partakers at an altar (1 Cor 10:18, 20; 2 Cor 1:7; 2 Pet 1:4).
Greek metochos (G3353) — a partaker, one who holds a share with another; Hebrews' word for partakers of Christ and of the heavenly calling (Heb 3:1, 14; 6:4; 12:8).
Greek koinōnia (G2842) — fellowship, communion, joint participation; the noun behind the communion of the blood of Christ (Acts 2:42; 1 Cor 10:16; 1 John 1:3).
usage: Partakers of the divine nature—real participation in God's holiness, not deification.
He that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds—the greeting is not neutral.
Communion is partaking: one cannot share the Lord's table and the table of devils.

etymology: From Latin subducere / subdere, to bring under; sub- (under) + a root of leading or placing. To subdue is to bring a thing under ordered rule—the placing of something beneath a rightful authority.
biblical_def: Subdue means to bring under rule, and in Scripture it is first a mandate, not a conquest. God blesses the first pair and commands, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion (Gen 1:28)—spoken before the fall, so subduing is not a consequence of sin but part of the original vocation of the image-bearer. The earth is to be brought under ordered, fruitful cultivation by creatures who are themselves under God. The word then follows the pattern of redemptive history. God subdues nations under His people (Ps 47:3), and—far more importantly—subdues His people's worst enemy: he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea (Mic 7:19). Paul turns the mandate inward: I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway (1 Cor 9:27)—the man commissioned to subdue the earth must first subdue himself, and an unsubdued preacher is a disqualified one. The horizon is Christ's: He is able even to subdue all things unto himself (Phil 3:21). So the word runs in a straight line from Eden to the last day: creatures under God subdue the earth; sin resists; Christ subdues sin, death, and finally all things, and hands the kingdom to the Father.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SUBDUE as to conquer and bring into permanent subjection; to overpower; also to tame, to soften, and to bring land under cultivation.
webster_full: SUBDUE, v.t. — To conquer by force or the exertion of superior power, and bring into permanent subjection; to reduce under dominion.
SUBDUE, v.t. — To overpower and destroy the force of; to tame; to soften; to subject to good order. Also, to break as land by plowing and harrowing, and render it mellow and fit for tillage.
scriptures: Genesis 1:28

And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth.
Micah 7:19
He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
1 Corinthians 9:27
But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.
Philippians 3:21
Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself.
corruption_summary: The dominion mandate is read today either as a license for exploitation or as an embarrassment to be apologized for, and both misreadings skip the governing fact: the creature commanded to subdue is himself under God and answerable for how he rules.
corruption_paragraphs: One corruption treats subdue as a warrant for extraction: the earth as raw material, dominion as ownership without accounting. Scripture forecloses it. The subduer is a steward under a Lord who retains title—the earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof—and stewards give account. Webster's agricultural sense is the closest analogy the older language preserved: to subdue land is to plow and harrow it until it is mellow and fit for tillage. That is cultivation for fruitfulness, not strip-mining.

The opposite corruption treats the mandate itself as the problem—dominion recast as the root of ecological and colonial sin, with the ideal human as one who touches nothing and shapes nothing. That is not humility but abdication, and it leaves the world to be shaped by whoever feels no such scruple. Meanwhile the inward sense has been largely abandoned. Paul subdues his own body first, and a culture that regards appetite as identity has no category for the self-subduing man—which is why it produces so many who would remake the world and cannot govern their own evenings.
roots_summary: Hebrew kabash, to bring into subjection or bondage; Greek hypotassō, to place under in ordered rank—dominion exercised by a creature who is himself under authority.
roots_lines: Hebrew kabash (H3533) — to subdue, bring into bondage, tread down; the verb of the creation mandate and of subduing land (Gen 1:28; Num 32:22, 29; Josh 18:1).
Greek hypotassō (G5293) — to place under, subject, subordinate in ordered rank; used of all things being subdued unto Christ (1 Cor 15:27-28; Phil 3:21; Heb 2:8).
Greek doulagōgeō (G1396) — to bring into slavery or subjection; Paul's word for what he does to his own body (1 Cor 9:27).
usage: Replenish the earth, and subdue it—a mandate given before the fall, not a consequence of it.
He will subdue our iniquities—the enemy God most needs to subdue is inside His people.
Paul subdues his own body first; an unsubdued preacher is a castaway.

etymology: Latin aestimare, to value or appraise—the same root that gives English estimate. To esteem is to set a price on a thing. The KJV keeps that commercial edge: esteeming is reckoning worth, and a man's esteem reveals his ledger.
biblical_def: Esteem is the act of reckoning worth, and Scripture is chiefly interested in whether a man's reckoning matches reality. The command in Philippians reverses the natural ledger: let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves (Phil 2:3)—not pretending others are more gifted, but assigning them a higher place than one assigns oneself, which is precisely what Christ did in the verses that follow. Moses is commended for an appraisal the world would call insane: esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt (Heb 11:26). He priced shame with the people of God above the wealth of an empire, and faith is what made the arithmetic work. The most sobering use is Isaiah's, and it is a valuation of Christ Himself: he was despised, and we esteemed him not (Isa 53:3). The world looked at the Servant and marked Him down to nothing; the whole doctrine of the cross runs through that misappraisal. Paul also commands esteem toward faithful leaders—to esteem them very highly in love for their work's sake (1 Thess 5:13)—esteem grounded in labor rather than charisma. Elsewhere he notes that one man esteemeth one day above another while another esteems every day alike (Rom 14:5), leaving room for conscience in things indifferent. The biblical question is never whether a man esteems, but whether he is pricing things as God prices them.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ESTEEM as to set a value on, whether high or low; to prize; and hence to regard with reverence or respect. The noun is the value or estimate set upon a person or thing.
webster_full: ESTEEM, v.t. — To set a value on, whether high or low; to estimate; to value. Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt (Heb 11:26).
ESTEEM, n. — The valuation or estimate set upon a person or thing; hence, high value or estimation; great regard; favorable opinion founded on supposed worth.
scriptures: Philippians 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
Hebrews 11:26
Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward.
Isaiah 53:3
He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
1 Thessalonians 5:13
And to esteem them very highly in love for their work's sake. And be at peace among yourselves.
corruption_summary: Esteem has been turned inward and made a therapeutic project—self-esteem as the foundation of well-being—inverting a word Scripture always points outward and upward, at God, at brothers, and at the reproach of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The self-esteem movement took a word for appraising worth and made the self both the appraiser and the object. Its promise was that a high self-valuation produces good outcomes; decades of research and ordinary observation have been unkind to that claim, and Scripture predicted the failure from a different direction. Philippians commands a man to esteem others better than themselves, which is not self-hatred—the same letter is full of joy and confidence—but a reordering of the ledger in which the self stops being the item under constant appraisal at all. Freedom lies there, not in a higher score.

The second corruption is the collapse of esteem into feeling. To esteem someone now means to like or admire him; in Scripture it means to assign him a place, with obligations attached. Paul's esteem them very highly in love for their work's sake concerns faithful labor, not personality, which is why esteem for elders survives an unimpressive manner and does not survive unfaithfulness. And Isaiah 53:3 stands as the permanent warning about crowd-sourced valuation: the whole world once appraised the Son of God and esteemed him not.
roots_summary: Hebrew chashab, to reckon or account, and bazah, to despise; Greek hēgeomai, to lead or count—the verb of Philippians 2:3, to count another higher.
roots_lines: Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to reckon, account, esteem, impute; the same accounting verb used of righteousness reckoned to Abraham (Gen 15:6; Isa 53:3-4).
Greek hēgeomai (G2233) — to lead, and hence to consider, count, esteem; used both of esteeming others better and of Paul counting all things loss for Christ (Phil 2:3, 6; 3:7-8).
Greek krinō (G2919) — to judge or discern; used in Romans 14:5 of the man who esteemeth one day above another.
usage: Let each esteem other better than themselves—a reordered ledger, not a lower self-score.
Moses priced the reproach of Christ above Egypt's treasury and called it the better deal.
He was despised, and we esteemed him not—the crowd's valuation of Christ was worthless.

etymology: Latin defraudare: de- (away) + fraudare (to cheat), from fraus, deceit. To defraud is to take away by deceit what is owed—the theft that hides inside a transaction.
biblical_def: To defraud is to deprive a man by deceit of what is rightly his. It is theft's respectable cousin: not the burglar's crowbar but the shorted wage, the shaved measure, the withheld due, the exploited advantage. Christ includes it in His summary of the commandments to the rich young ruler: Do not defraud (Mark 10:19), setting it alongside murder, adultery, and theft. Paul rebukes the Corinthians for suing one another and adds that even winning is losing: Nay, ye do wrong, and defraud, and that your brethren (1 Cor 6:8). The word governs the marriage bed as well: Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time (1 Cor 7:5)—the conjugal due is owed, and withholding it is classified not as preference but as fraud. Most striking is 1 Thessalonians 4:6, where defraud lands in the sexual lane: that no man go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter: because that the Lord is the avenger of all such. Sexual sin is there framed as robbing another man—of a wife, of a daughter, of a future spouse's purity—with God Himself named as the avenger of the debt. James adds the employer's version: wages kept back by fraud cry out, and the cries have entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth (Jas 5:4). In every case the injured party may not even know; the ledger is kept in heaven.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DEFRAUD as to deprive of right, either by obtaining something by deception or artifice, or by taking something wrongfully without the knowledge or consent of the owner.
webster_full: DEFRAUD, v.t. — To deprive of right, either by obtaining something by deception or artifice, or by taking something wrongfully without the knowledge or consent of the owner; to cheat; to cozen.
DEFRAUD, v.t. — To withhold wrongfully from another what is due to him. Defraud not thy neighbor, neither rob him: the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night (Lev 19:13).
scriptures: 1 Thessalonians 4:6
That no man go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter: because that the Lord is the avenger of all such, as we also have forewarned you and testified.
1 Corinthians 6:8
Nay, ye do wrong, and defraud, and that your brethren.
1 Corinthians 7:5
Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency.
Mark 10:19
