Thou knowest the commandments, Do not commit adultery, Do not kill, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Defraud not, Honour thy father and mother.
corruption_summary: Consent has replaced obligation as the only moral test, so that any arrangement both parties agreed to is presumed harmless—which erases fraud in exactly the areas Scripture applies the word most sharply: wages, sexual conduct, and dealings between brothers.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing modern rule is that where there is consent there is no victim. Scripture works from obligation rather than agreement: a wage is owed, a conjugal due is owed, a brother is owed honest dealing, and these debts do not evaporate because both parties signed. That is why James can indict employers whose contracts were perfectly legal and whose withheld wages still cry out to God, and why Paul can call a lawsuit victory over a brother a defrauding even when the court agreed.

The sexual application is the one most thoroughly lost. First Thessalonians 4 places sexual sin under the heading of fraud—going beyond and defrauding a brother—because immorality takes from someone: a husband, a father, a future spouse, a congregation. The contemporary frame recognizes only the two adults present and their agreement, so the defrauded third parties become invisible. Paul answers with the plainest possible warning: the Lord is the avenger of all such. The debt is recorded even when no human plaintiff ever appears.
roots_summary: Hebrew ashaq, to oppress or extort; Greek apostereō, to rob or withhold what is due, and pleonekteō, to take advantage by greed.
roots_lines: Hebrew ashaq (H6231) — to oppress, defraud, extort; used of withholding a hired man's wages and of oppressing the poor (Lev 19:13; Deut 24:14; Mal 3:5).
Greek apostereō (G650) — to defraud, deprive, withhold what is owed; used of lawsuits between brothers and of the conjugal due (Mark 10:19; 1 Cor 6:7-8; 7:5; Jas 5:4).
Greek pleonekteō (G4122) — to overreach, take advantage of, exploit through covetousness; the verb of 1 Thess 4:6 (2 Cor 2:11; 7:2; 12:17-18).
usage: Do not defraud—Christ lists it with murder, adultery, and theft.
1 Thessalonians 4:6 files sexual sin under fraud: someone is being robbed, and God avenges.
1 Corinthians 7:5 makes the conjugal due a debt; withholding it is not preference but fraud.

etymology: Latin confundere: con- (together) + fundere (to pour)—to pour together, to mix into disorder. From the mixing sense comes the second: to be thrown into disorder is to be put to shame, and the KJV uses both.
biblical_def: Confound carries two joined senses in the KJV: to mix into confusion, and to put to shame. The first is Babel, where God says, let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another's speech (Gen 11:7)—a judgment executed by mixing, the one unified rebel project broken by making speech unintelligible. The Hebrew wordplay is deliberate: the place is called Babel because there the LORD confounded the language. Pentecost is the deliberate reversal, where men of every tongue hear the wonderful works of God in their own language, and the multitude is again confounded, this time by grace rather than judgment. The shame sense runs through the prophets and the Psalms: let me never be confounded is the repeated prayer of the man who has trusted God publicly and would be humiliated if God failed. Peter applies it to Christ: he that believeth on him shall not be confounded (1 Pet 2:6). Paul then makes confounding an instrument of the gospel's strategy: God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty (1 Cor 1:27). And the whole is bounded by a rule about God's own character: God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints (1 Cor 14:33). God confounds rebels; He does not run His church that way.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CONFOUND as to mingle and blend so that things cannot be distinguished; to throw into disorder; to perplex; and to abash or put to shame.
webster_full: CONFOUND, v.t. — To mingle and blend different things, so that their forms or natures cannot be distinguished; to mix in a mass or crowd, so that individuals cannot be discerned.
CONFOUND, v.t. — To perplex; to disconcert; to abash; to throw the mind into disorder. Hence, to put to shame. He that believeth on him shall not be confounded (1 Pet 2:6).
scriptures: Genesis 11:7
Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another's speech.
1 Corinthians 1:27
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
1 Corinthians 14:33
For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
1 Peter 2:6
Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded.
corruption_summary: Confusion has been promoted from a judgment to a virtue—ambiguity as sophistication, the blurring of categories as progress—while confounded as public shame has faded, taking with it the force of the promise that the believer shall never be put to shame.
corruption_paragraphs: The Babel sense is worth holding onto because the modern instinct is to treat category confusion as maturity. Clear distinctions—between male and female, between the church and the world, between truth and preference—are described as simplistic, and the mixing of them as nuance. Genesis 11 says confounding was God's judicial act against a project of unified rebellion, and 1 Corinthians 14:33 says God is not the author of confusion in His churches. A church that cultivates ambiguity as its house style is imitating the judgment rather than the peace.

The shame sense has quietly disappeared, and its loss costs the believer a promise. To be confounded in Scripture is to have publicly trusted and been publicly humiliated—the terror behind let me never be confounded. Peter's assurance that the one who believes on Christ shall not be confounded is therefore not a statement about feelings but about the last day: the man who staked everything on this cornerstone will not be exposed as a fool. Modern confounded means merely puzzled, which reduces a promise about vindication to a remark about confusion.
roots_summary: Hebrew balal, to mix or confuse, the Babel verb, and bosh, to be ashamed; Greek kataischynō, to put to shame or disgrace.
roots_lines: Hebrew balal (H1101) — to mix, mingle, confuse; the verb behind the name Babel (Gen 11:7, 9).
Hebrew bosh (H954) — to be ashamed, disappointed, put to confusion; the psalmist's let me never be put to confusion (Ps 22:5; 31:1; 71:1; Isa 45:17).
Greek kataischynō (G2617) — to dishonor, put to shame, disgrace; used of God confounding the wise and of the believer never being confounded (Rom 5:5; 9:33; 1 Cor 1:27; 1 Pet 2:6).
usage: There confound their language—Babel: confusion as a judicial act of God.
God is not the author of confusion, but of peace—the rule for His churches.
He that believeth on him shall not be confounded—a promise of vindication, not of clarity.

etymology: From re- (again) + new, on the model of Latin renovare. To renew is to make new again—which in Scripture is always the work of a hand outside the thing being renewed.
biblical_def: Renew means to make new again, and the decisive biblical point is that the renewer is God and the renewed is passive under His work. David asks for it rather than achieving it: Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me (Ps 51:10)—create and renew in parallel, both verbs God's. Isaiah promises it to the waiting: they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles (Isa 40:31), where the strength comes precisely to those who stop generating it themselves. Paul locates Christian transformation in a renewed mind: be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind (Rom 12:2)—and the renewing is the mechanism, not a mood. Ephesians repeats it: be renewed in the spirit of your mind (Eph 4:23), set between putting off the old man and putting on the new. And there is the daily arithmetic of 2 Corinthians, written by a man being worn out in ministry: though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day (2 Cor 4:16). Two ledgers run at once—the body declining, the inner man renewed—and only one of them is visible. Covenant is renewed too: Israel gathers at Shechem, at the Water Gate, under Josiah, to hear the law read and take the covenant again, which is the corporate form of the same act.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines RENEW as to make new again, to restore to a former state or to a good state after decay; and in theology, to renovate the heart by the Holy Spirit, implanting holy affections.
webster_full: RENEW, v.t. — To renovate; to restore to a former state, or to a good state, after decay or depravation; to rebuild; to repair.

RENEW, v.t. — In theology, to make new; to renovate; to transform; to change from natural enmity to the love of God and his law; to implant holy affections in the heart. Be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind (Rom 12:2).
scriptures: Romans 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
2 Corinthians 4:16
For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
Psalm 51:10
Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
Isaiah 40:31
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
corruption_summary: Renewal has been absorbed into the wellness market as a self-administered reset—retreat, cleanse, rebrand, fresh start—replacing the biblical pattern in which repentance comes first and the renewing is done by God, not by the man.
corruption_paragraphs: The market sells renewal as a product a man applies to himself: the reset, the detox, the sabbatical, the new year's version of a new self. Every one of these is self-administered, and none requires repentance. Romans 12:2 is regularly recruited into this scheme as though the renewing of the mind were a program of positive input the believer runs. The grammar refuses it: be ye transformed is passive, the renewing is God's operation by His Spirit and His Word, and the sentence sits after eleven chapters of doctrine and the word therefore. It is not a spa; it is what mercy produces.

The second corruption is the demand that renewal be visible and immediate. Paul's actual account is stranger and more useful: the outward man is perishing while the inward man is renewed day by day—renewal running alongside decline, incrementally, with the visible ledger going the wrong direction the whole time. A generation trained to expect transformation as a photographable event has no framework for the aging saint who is being renewed daily and cannot show it, which is exactly the condition most Christians live in.
roots_summary: Hebrew chadash, to renew or repair; Greek anakainōsis, a renewing that makes qualitatively new—the noun of Romans 12:2.
roots_lines: Hebrew chadash (H2318) — to renew, repair, restore; used of renewing the kingdom, repairing the temple, and renewing strength (1 Sam 11:14; 2 Chr 24:4; Ps 51:10; Isa 40:31).
Greek anakainōsis (G342) — a renewal, renovation, complete change for the better; used only of the renewing of the mind and of the washing of regeneration (Rom 12:2; Titus 3:5).
Greek anakainoō (G341) — to make new again, renew; the daily renewing of the inward man (2 Cor 4:16; Col 3:10).
usage: Renew a right spirit within me—David asks; he does not perform it.
Transformed by the renewing of your mind—passive voice, God's operation, after therefore.
The inward man is renewed day by day—renewal running under visible decline.

etymology: From en- (in) + camp, from Latin campus, a field. To encamp is to pitch in a field as an army or a host—an ordered settlement with a center, a perimeter, and a commander.
biblical_def: To encamp is to pitch as an army or a host, and in Scripture it is never a random bivouac. Israel in the wilderness encamps by a published order: every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house: far off about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch (Num 2:2). Three tribes to a side, the Levites ringing the center, the tabernacle in the middle—a camp shaped as a theological statement, with God dwelling at the center of an ordered people. The camp moves when the cloud moves and stops when it stops; even the sanitation laws of Deuteronomy are grounded in the fact that the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp. God Himself takes up the posture. The angel of God that went before the camp of Israel removed and went behind them at the Red Sea (Exod 14:19), the divine escort repositioning to guard the rear where the danger was. Zechariah has the LORD saying, I will encamp about mine house because of the army (Zech 9:8). And the promise every believer remembers: the angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them (Ps 34:7)—not a vague sense of protection but a military perimeter, established around a specific class of people, those who fear Him. Hebrews then takes the camp language and turns it: Christ suffered without the gate, and believers are called to go forth unto Him without the camp, bearing his reproach.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ENCAMP as to pitch tents or form huts, as an army; to halt on a march and place in order for rest or defense; and transitively, to form into a camp.

ENCAMP, v.t. — To form into a camp; to place a marching army or company in a temporary habitation or quarters. The angel of the Lord encampeth round about them that fear him (Ps 34:7).

corruption_summary: Rootlessness is now sold as freedom—the man with no fixed address, no assigned place, no standard to pitch by—while Scripture's camp is ordered, located, and centered on the presence of God, with protection promised to a people who can be found.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ideal is mobility: unattached, remote, able to relocate on a week's notice, belonging to no particular congregation or town. Numbers 2 describes the opposite arrangement. Every man pitches by his own standard, with the ensign of his father's house—he has a tribe, a position, a side of the tabernacle, and neighbors who notice if his tent is missing. The camp was portable, so this is not an argument against ever moving; it is an argument that even a people on the march were ordered, assigned, and accountable while they moved.

The second loss is the perimeter. Psalm 34:7 promises that the angel of the LORD encamps round about them that fear him—a guarded circumference around an identifiable people, not a diffuse benevolence over everyone. Spiritualize the camp away and the promise becomes a sentiment. Keep it, and it stays military: God posts a guard around a located people, and Exodus 14 shows Him moving that guard to whichever side the enemy is on.
roots_summary: Hebrew chanah, to pitch a tent, encamp, or lay siege—the same verb for Israel's ordered camp and for the LORD's guard around His own.
roots_lines: Hebrew chanah (H2583) — to decline, pitch a tent, encamp; used of Israel's tribal camps, of besieging armies, and of the angel of the LORD encamping around the God-fearing (Exod 13:20; Num 2:2; Ps 34:7; Zech 9:8).
Hebrew machaneh (H4264) — a camp, host, or company; the noun behind Mahanaim, two camps (Gen 32:2; Exod 14:19; Deut 23:14).
Greek parembolē (G3925) — a camp or barracks; Hebrews' word in the call to go forth unto Christ without the camp (Acts 21:34; Heb 13:11-13).
